items.stem: Define the term "standard entropy (S⦵)".
items.answer: The entropy of one mole of a substance under standard conditions, in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; always positive above 0 K
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the entropy of one mole of a substance under standard conditions, in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; always positive above 0 K. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: "The standard entropy of O₂(g) is zero because it is an element." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Standard entropies are absolute and positive (O₂ 205 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹); only ΔHf of elements is defined as zero.
items.markingKey: Standard entropies are absolute and positive (O₂ 205 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹); only ΔHf of elements is defined as zero. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Predict and explain the sign of the entropy change for the thermite reaction, 2Al(s) + Fe₂O₃(s) → Al₂O₃(s) + 2Fe(s).
items.answer: negative (−38.0 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹): the number of moles of gas does not change, so ΔS is small and its sign depends on the S⦵ values.
items.markingKey: sign − (1); the number of moles of gas does not change, so ΔS is small and its sign depends on the S⦵ values – gases have much higher entropy than solids/liquids (1).

items.stem: Predict the sign of ΔS for 2CO(g) + O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g).
options: positive: the number of moles of gas decreases
negative: the number of moles of gas decreases
negative: the number of moles of gas increases
items.answer: negative: the number of moles of gas decreases
items.markingKey: B. Gas moles change by −1.

items.stem: Calculate ΔS⦵ for the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g). Standard entropies / J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹: CaCO₃(s) 93, CaO(s) 40, CO₂(g) 214.
items.answer: +161 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: ΣS(products) = 254, ΣS(reactants) = 93 (M1, coefficients used); ΔS = +161 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (A1).

items.stem: Ammonium nitrate dissolves in water spontaneously although the process is endothermic (ΔH = +25.7 kJ mol⁻¹). (a) Explain, in terms of entropy, why the process is spontaneous. (b) Estimate the minimum ΔS needed at 298 K. (c) Suggest why the temperature of the solution falls.
items.answer: (a) ions leave the ordered lattice and disperse – large increase in entropy of the system outweighs the decrease in entropy of the surroundings (heat absorbed). (b) ΔS > ΔH/T = 25700/298 = 86 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. (c) energy absorbed from the water to break the lattice is greater than released by hydration.
items.markingKey: (a) ions leave the ordered lattice and disperse – large increase in entropy of the system outweighs the decrease in entropy of the surroundings (heat absorbed). (b) ΔS > ΔH/T = 25700/298 = 86 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. (c) energy absorbed from the water to break the lattice is greater than released by hydration.

items.stem: Why is the standard entropy of an element not zero, unlike its enthalpy of formation?
options: Entropy is an absolute quantity that is zero only for a perfect crystal at 0 K.
items.answer: Entropy is an absolute quantity that is zero only for a perfect crystal at 0 K.
items.markingKey: A. Third law.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The difference between the total entropy of the products and that of the reactants: ΔS = ΣS(products) − ΣS(reactants)"?
items.answer: entropy change (ΔS)
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of entropy change (ΔS).

items.stem: Explain why the entropy of a substance increases when it melts.
items.answer: In the liquid the particles are more disordered and can move past each other, so there are many more possible arrangements of particles and energy than in the ordered solid.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: In the liquid the particles are more disordered and can move past each other, so there are many more possible arrangements of particles and energy than in the ordered solid. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between enthalpy and entropy.
items.answer: Entropy (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) measures the dispersal of matter and energy; enthalpy (kJ mol⁻¹) measures heat content – a reaction’s spontaneity depends on both via ΔG.
items.markingKey: Entropy (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) measures the dispersal of matter and energy; enthalpy (kJ mol⁻¹) measures heat content – a reaction’s spontaneity depends on both via ΔG. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: For 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l), ΔS is
items.answer: large and negative
items.markingKey: B. 3 mol gas → liquid.

items.stem: Explain why dissolving sodium chloride in water increases entropy.
items.answer: The ions leave the ordered lattice and become dispersed through the solution, increasing the number of possible arrangements (outweighing the ordering of water molecules around the ions).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The ions leave the ordered lattice and become dispersed through the solution, increasing the number of possible arrangements (outweighing the ordering of water molecules around the ions). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: What is ΔS⦵ for the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide: 2H₂O₂(l) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g). Standard entropies / J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹: H₂O₂(l) 110, H₂O(l) 70, O₂(g) 205.
items.answer: +125 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: A. ΔS = ΣS(products) − ΣS(reactants) = +125 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

items.stem: Calculate ΔS⦵ for the combustion of ethanol: C₂H₅OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l). Standard entropies / J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹: C₂H₅OH(l) 161, O₂(g) 205, CO₂(g) 214, H₂O(l) 70.
items.answer: −138 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: ΣS(products) = 638, ΣS(reactants) = 776 (M1, coefficients used); ΔS = −138 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (A1).

items.stem: Calculate ΔS⦵ for the combustion of methane: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l). Standard entropies / J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹: CH₄(g) 186, O₂(g) 205, CO₂(g) 214, H₂O(l) 70.
items.answer: −242 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: D. ΣS(products) = 354, ΣS(reactants) = 596 (M1, coefficients used); ΔS = −242 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (A1).

items.stem: Predict the sign of ΔS for 2NO₂(g) → N₂O₄(g).
options: negative: the number of moles of gas decreases
negative: the number of moles of gas increases
positive: the number of moles of gas decreases
items.answer: negative: the number of moles of gas decreases
items.markingKey: A. Gas moles change by −1.

items.stem: Consider (I) CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g) and (II) 2H₂O₂(l) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g). (a) Predict the sign of ΔS for each, giving reasons. (b) Calculate ΔS⦵ for each using the data booklet standard entropies. (c) Explain which reaction shows the greater increase in disorder, and whether your predictions in (a) were correct.
items.answer: (b) I +161 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, II +125 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: (a) signs predicted from change in moles of gas/states (R1 R1). (b) I = +161, II = +125 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (A1 A1). (c) I has the more positive ΔS; comparison with predictions (R1).

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Counting moles of gas is a reliable way to predict the sign of ΔS for a reaction."
items.answer: A good first approximation, but calculations with S⦵ values are needed when gas moles are equal or effects compete.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: gas entropy dominates, so the rule works for most reactions; quick qualitative prediction. Arguments against: fails when the number of gas moles is unchanged; dissolving, mixing and changes in molecular complexity also matter; quantitative ΔS requires standard entropies. Supported judgement: A good first approximation, but calculations with S⦵ values are needed when gas moles are equal or effects compete. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: Define the term "spontaneous reaction".
items.answer: A reaction that, once started, proceeds without continuous external input of energy; ΔG < 0 (it may still be very slow)
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a reaction that, once started, proceeds without continuous external input of energy; ΔG < 0 (it may still be very slow). Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: A student claims: "If ΔG is negative the reaction goes to completion." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Negative ΔG⦵ means K > 1 and products are favoured at equilibrium, but the reaction still reaches equilibrium rather than completion.
items.markingKey: Negative ΔG⦵ means K > 1 and products are favoured at equilibrium, but the reaction still reaches equilibrium rather than completion. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Which combination gives a reaction that is spontaneous only at high temperatures?
items.answer: ΔH > 0, ΔS > 0
items.markingKey: C. TΔS must exceed ΔH.

items.stem: For the combustion of methane, CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), ΔH⦵ = −892 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS⦵ = −242 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. What is ΔG at 400 K?
items.answer: −795 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: D. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = −892 − 400 × (−242/1000) = −795 kJ mol⁻¹. Forgetting to convert J to kJ is the common error.

items.stem: For the extraction of zinc by carbon, ZnO(s) + C(s) → Zn(s) + CO(g), ΔH⦵ = +239 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS⦵ = +190.3 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. What is ΔG at 1000 K?
items.answer: +48.7 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: B. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = 239 − 1000 × (190.3/1000) = +48.7 kJ mol⁻¹. Forgetting to convert J to kJ is the common error.

items.stem: For the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide, 2H₂O₂(l) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g), ΔH⦵ = −196 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS⦵ = +125 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Calculate ΔG at 800 K and state whether the reaction is spontaneous at this temperature.
items.answer: −296 kJ mol⁻¹; spontaneous
items.markingKey: ΔS converted to +0.125 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (M1); ΔG = −196 − 800(+0.125) = −296 kJ mol⁻¹ (A1); spontaneous because ΔG < 0 (A1).

items.stem:
Consider the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g).

species | ΔHf⦵ / kJ mol⁻¹ | S⦵ / J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
CaCO₃(s) | −1207 | 93
CaO(s) | −635 | 40
CO₂(g) | −394 | 214

(a) Calculate ΔH⦵. (b) Calculate ΔS⦵. (c) Calculate ΔG at 298 K and deduce whether the reaction is spontaneous. (d) Calculate the temperature at which the reaction becomes (or stops being) spontaneous.
items.answer: (a) +178 kJ mol⁻¹; (b) +161 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; (c) +130 kJ mol⁻¹, not spontaneous; (d) 1110 K
items.markingKey: (a) ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants) = +178 (A1). (b) +161 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (A1). (c) ΔG = ΔH − TΔS with ΔS in kJ (M1) = +130 kJ mol⁻¹ (A1). (d) T = ΔH/ΔS = 178/0.161 = 1110 K (A1).

items.stem: "ΔG⦵ values are sufficient to decide whether an industrial process is viable." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: ΔG⦵ is a necessary first screen, but kinetics, equilibrium position under real conditions and economics decide viability.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: identify feasible reactions and favourable temperatures; link to equilibrium constants. Arguments against: rates may be far too slow without catalysts; real conditions are non-standard; costs, safety, yield and environmental factors are also decisive. Supported judgement: ΔG⦵ is a necessary first screen, but kinetics, equilibrium position under real conditions and economics decide viability. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Gibbs energy change (ΔG)"?
options: The entropy of one mole of a substance under standard conditions, in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; always positive above 0 K
The energy change that combines enthalpy and entropy, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS; a reaction is spontaneous (thermodynamically favourable) when ΔG is negative
The temperature T = ΔH/ΔS at which ΔG = 0, above or below which the spontaneity of a reaction changes sign
A reaction that, once started, proceeds without continuous external input of energy; ΔG < 0 (it may still be very slow)
items.answer: The energy change that combines enthalpy and entropy, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS; a reaction is spontaneous (thermodynamically favourable) when ΔG is negative
items.markingKey: B. "Gibbs energy change (ΔG)" is the energy change that combines enthalpy and entropy, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS; a reaction is spontaneous (thermodynamically favourable) when ΔG is negative.

items.stem: Why must ΔS be divided by 1000 when using ΔG = ΔH − TΔS with ΔH in kJ mol⁻¹?
options: ΔS is usually given in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
items.answer: ΔS is usually given in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
items.markingKey: A. Units must match.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a negative ΔG does not mean that a reaction will be observed to occur quickly.
items.answer: ΔG indicates thermodynamic feasibility only; the rate depends on the activation energy, so a spontaneous reaction may be extremely slow (e.g. diamond → graphite).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: ΔG indicates thermodynamic feasibility only; the rate depends on the activation energy, so a spontaneous reaction may be extremely slow (e.g. diamond → graphite). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a fast reaction and a spontaneous reaction.
items.answer: Spontaneity (ΔG < 0) concerns whether a reaction is thermodynamically favourable; speed concerns kinetics (activation energy); they are independent.
items.markingKey: Spontaneity (ΔG < 0) concerns whether a reaction is thermodynamically favourable; speed concerns kinetics (activation energy); they are independent. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A reaction has ΔH = −100 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = −200 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. At which temperatures is it spontaneous?
items.answer: below 500 K
items.markingKey: D. ΔG < 0 when T < ΔH/ΔS = 500 K.

items.stem: Briefly explain why ΔG combines both the system and the surroundings.
items.answer: ΔH/T represents the entropy change of the surroundings due to heat transfer; −ΔG/T = ΔS(system) + ΔS(surroundings) = ΔS(total), which must be positive for a spontaneous change.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: ΔH/T represents the entropy change of the surroundings due to heat transfer; −ΔG/T = ΔS(system) + ΔS(surroundings) = ΔS(total), which must be positive for a spontaneous change. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between a spontaneous reaction and a fast reaction.
items.answer: Spontaneity (ΔG < 0) concerns whether a reaction is thermodynamically favourable; speed concerns kinetics (activation energy); they are independent.
items.markingKey: Spontaneity (ΔG < 0) concerns whether a reaction is thermodynamically favourable; speed concerns kinetics (activation energy); they are independent. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: For the reduction of iron(III) oxide by carbon monoxide, Fe₂O₃(s) + 3CO(g) → 2Fe(s) + 3CO₂(g), ΔH⦵ = −25 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS⦵ = +15 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. What is ΔG at 298 K?
items.answer: −29.5 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: D. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = −25 − 298 × (15/1000) = −29.5 kJ mol⁻¹. Forgetting to convert J to kJ is the common error.

items.stem: For the hydrogenation of ethene, C₂H₄(g) + H₂(g) → C₂H₆(g), ΔH⦵ = −136 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS⦵ = −121 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Calculate ΔG at 1200 K and state whether the reaction is spontaneous at this temperature.
items.answer: +9.20 kJ mol⁻¹; not spontaneous
items.markingKey: ΔS converted to −0.121 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (M1); ΔG = −136 − 1200(−0.121) = +9.20 kJ mol⁻¹ (A1); not spontaneous because ΔG > 0 (A1).

items.stem: For the dimerisation of nitrogen dioxide, 2NO₂(g) → N₂O₄(g), ΔH⦵ = −57 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS⦵ = −176 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. What is ΔG at 800 K?
items.answer: +83.8 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: A. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = −57 − 800 × (−176/1000) = +83.8 kJ mol⁻¹. Forgetting to convert J to kJ is the common error.

items.stem: For the Contact process, 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g), ΔH⦵ = −198 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS⦵ = −187 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Calculate ΔG at 400 K and state whether the reaction is spontaneous at this temperature.
items.answer: −123 kJ mol⁻¹; spontaneous
items.markingKey: ΔS converted to −0.187 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (M1); ΔG = −198 − 400(−0.187) = −123 kJ mol⁻¹ (A1); spontaneous because ΔG < 0 (A1).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "ΔG⦵ = −RT ln K"?
options: The energy change that combines enthalpy and entropy, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS; a reaction is spontaneous (thermodynamically favourable) when ΔG is negative
The temperature T = ΔH/ΔS at which ΔG = 0, above or below which the spontaneity of a reaction changes sign
The relationship between the standard Gibbs energy change and the equilibrium constant at temperature T
A measure of the dispersal of energy and matter in a system: the number of possible arrangements of particles and their energy
items.answer: The relationship between the standard Gibbs energy change and the equilibrium constant at temperature T
items.markingKey: C. "ΔG⦵ = −RT ln K" is the relationship between the standard Gibbs energy change and the equilibrium constant at temperature T.

items.stem: For an exothermic reaction with a decrease in entropy, increasing the temperature
options: makes ΔG more negative and raises K
makes ΔG less negative and lowers K
items.answer: makes ΔG less negative and lowers K
items.markingKey: D. −TΔS is positive.

items.stem: A student claims: "At equilibrium ΔG⦵ = 0." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: At equilibrium ΔG = 0; ΔG⦵ is a fixed value for the reaction at that temperature and equals −RT ln K.
items.markingKey: At equilibrium ΔG = 0; ΔG⦵ is a fixed value for the reaction at that temperature and equals −RT ln K. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: For C(s) + CO₂(g) → 2CO(g), ΔH⦵ = +172 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS⦵ = +176.3 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. What is the temperature above which the reaction is spontaneous?
For CuO(s) + H₂(g) → Cu(s) + H₂O(l), ΔH⦵ = −129 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS⦵ = −71 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Determine the temperature below which the reaction is spontaneous.
items.markingKey: Set ΔG = 0: T = ΔH/ΔS (M1) = −129/−0.071 (unit conversion) = 1820 K (A1); spontaneous below this temperature (A1).

items.stem: The industrial reduction of zinc oxide by carbon, ZnO(s) + C(s) → Zn(s) + CO(g), has ΔH⦵ = +239 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS⦵ = +190 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. (a) Show that the reaction is not spontaneous at 298 K. (b) Calculate the minimum temperature for the reaction to be spontaneous. (c) Explain why a much higher temperature than this is used in practice.
items.answer: (a) ΔG = 239 − 298(0.190) = +182 kJ mol⁻¹ > 0. (b) T = 239/0.190 = 1260 K. (c) faster rate; zinc is removed as vapour (above b.p. 1180 K), shifting the equilibrium; ΔH and ΔS vary with temperature.
items.markingKey: (a) ΔG = 239 − 298(0.190) = +182 kJ mol⁻¹ > 0. (b) T = 239/0.190 = 1260 K. (c) faster rate; zinc is removed as vapour (above b.p. 1180 K), shifting the equilibrium; ΔH and ΔS vary with temperature.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The temperature T = ΔH/ΔS at which ΔG = 0, above or below which the spontaneity of a reaction changes sign"?
items.answer: crossover temperature
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of crossover temperature.

items.stem: If ΔG⦵ is large and negative, what can be deduced about K?
items.markingKey: D. ΔG⦵ = −RT ln K.

items.stem: For the combustion of ethanol, ΔH⦵ = −1368 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS⦵ = −138 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Explain how temperature affects the spontaneity of the reaction.
items.answer: Spontaneous only below 9910 K: at high T the positive −TΔS term outweighs the negative ΔH.
items.markingKey: Uses ΔG = ΔH − TΔS (1); spontaneous only below 9910 K: at high T the positive −TΔS term outweighs the negative ΔH (2).

items.stem: Explain the relationship between the sign of ΔG⦵ and the position of equilibrium.
items.answer: Since ΔG⦵ = −RT ln K, a negative ΔG⦵ gives ln K > 0 so K > 1 and products predominate; positive ΔG⦵ gives K < 1 and reactants predominate.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Since ΔG⦵ = −RT ln K, a negative ΔG⦵ gives ln K > 0 so K > 1 and products predominate; positive ΔG⦵ gives K < 1 and reactants predominate. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between ΔG⦵ and ΔG.
items.answer: ΔG⦵ refers to standard conditions (all species at standard state) and determines K; ΔG refers to the actual mixture and becomes zero at equilibrium.
items.markingKey: ΔG⦵ refers to standard conditions (all species at standard state) and determines K; ΔG refers to the actual mixture and becomes zero at equilibrium. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: At 700 K, ΔG⦵ for 2NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g) is −11.1 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the equilibrium constant K at this temperature and comment on the position of equilibrium. (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
items.answer: K = 6.74; products favoured

items.stem: Mohammed writes: "At equilibrium ΔG⦵ = 0." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: At equilibrium ΔG = 0; ΔG⦵ is a fixed value for the reaction at that temperature and equals −RT ln K.
items.markingKey: At equilibrium ΔG = 0; ΔG⦵ is a fixed value for the reaction at that temperature and equals −RT ln K. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g), ΔH⦵ = −92 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS⦵ = −199 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Determine the temperature below which the reaction is spontaneous.
items.markingKey: Set ΔG = 0: T = ΔH/ΔS (M1) = −92/−0.199 (unit conversion) = 462 K (A1); spontaneous below this temperature (A1).

items.stem: For 2Al(s) + Fe₂O₃(s) → Al₂O₃(s) + 2Fe(s), ΔH⦵ = −852 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS⦵ = −38 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Determine the temperature below which the reaction is spontaneous.
items.markingKey: A. Set ΔG = 0: T = ΔH/ΔS (M1) = −852/−0.038 (unit conversion) = 22400 K (A1); spontaneous below this temperature (A1).

items.stem: For 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s), ΔH⦵ = −1204 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS⦵ = −217 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Determine the temperature below which the reaction is spontaneous.
items.markingKey: D. Set ΔG = 0: T = ΔH/ΔS (M1) = −1204/−0.217 (unit conversion) = 5550 K (A1); spontaneous below this temperature (A1).

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Increasing the temperature always makes reactions more spontaneous."
items.answer: The effect depends on the sign of ΔS: higher temperatures favour entropy-increasing reactions only.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: true for reactions with positive ΔS; higher temperatures also increase rate. Arguments against: for reactions with negative ΔS, higher T makes ΔG less negative; exothermic equilibria shift left at higher T. Supported judgement: The effect depends on the sign of ΔS: higher temperatures favour entropy-increasing reactions only. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: For the combustion of methane, CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), ΔH⦵ = −892 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS⦵ = −242 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. (a) Calculate ΔG⦵ at 298 K and at 2550 K. (b) Determine the temperature at which ΔG⦵ = 0. (c) Explain how the equilibrium constant changes as the temperature passes this value. (d) Comment on the assumption that ΔH and ΔS do not change with temperature.
items.answer: (a) −820 and −275 kJ mol⁻¹; (b) 3690 K
items.markingKey: (a) −820 kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K and −275 kJ mol⁻¹ at 2550 K (A1 A1). (b) T = ΔH/ΔS = 3690 K (A1). (c) K passes from >1 to <1 since ΔG⦵ = −RT ln K (R1). (d) both vary slightly with T, so the calculated temperature is an estimate (R1).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A reaction that, once started, proceeds without continuous external input of energy; ΔG < 0 (it may still be very slow)"?
items.answer: spontaneous reaction
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of spontaneous reaction.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "standard entropy (S⦵)"?
options: A reaction that, once started, proceeds without continuous external input of energy; ΔG < 0 (it may still be very slow)
A negative ΔG⦵ corresponds to K > 1 (products favoured); a positive ΔG⦵ corresponds to K < 1 (reactants favoured)
The entropy of one mole of a substance under standard conditions, in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; always positive above 0 K
The energy change that combines enthalpy and entropy, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS; a reaction is spontaneous (thermodynamically favourable) when ΔG is negative
items.answer: The entropy of one mole of a substance under standard conditions, in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; always positive above 0 K
items.markingKey: C. "standard entropy (S⦵)" is the entropy of one mole of a substance under standard conditions, in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; always positive above 0 K.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "position of equilibrium and ΔG".
items.answer: A negative ΔG⦵ corresponds to K > 1 (products favoured); a positive ΔG⦵ corresponds to K < 1 (reactants favoured)
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a negative ΔG⦵ corresponds to K > 1 (products favoured); a positive ΔG⦵ corresponds to K < 1 (reactants favoured). Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between a spontaneous reaction and a fast reaction.
items.answer: Spontaneity (ΔG < 0) concerns whether a reaction is thermodynamically favourable; speed concerns kinetics (activation energy); they are independent.
items.markingKey: Spontaneity (ΔG < 0) concerns whether a reaction is thermodynamically favourable; speed concerns kinetics (activation energy); they are independent. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between enthalpy and entropy.
items.answer: Entropy (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) measures the dispersal of matter and energy; enthalpy (kJ mol⁻¹) measures heat content – a reaction’s spontaneity depends on both via ΔG.
items.markingKey: Entropy (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) measures the dispersal of matter and energy; enthalpy (kJ mol⁻¹) measures heat content – a reaction’s spontaneity depends on both via ΔG. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why the Haber process becomes less thermodynamically favourable at high temperature.
items.answer: ΔH is negative and ΔS is negative; as T rises, −TΔS becomes a larger positive term, so ΔG becomes less negative and eventually positive (above about 460 K); K decreases.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: ΔH is negative and ΔS is negative; as T rises, −TΔS becomes a larger positive term, so ΔG becomes less negative and eventually positive (above about 460 K); K decreases. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "All exothermic reactions are spontaneous." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: An exothermic reaction with a large negative ΔS may have positive ΔG at high temperature (e.g. N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ above about 460 K).
items.markingKey: An exothermic reaction with a large negative ΔS may have positive ΔG at high temperature (e.g. N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ above about 460 K). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Predict and explain the sign of the entropy change for the Contact process, 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g).
items.answer: negative (−187 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹): gas moles change from 3 to 2.
items.markingKey: sign − (1); gas moles change from 3 to 2 – gases have much higher entropy than solids/liquids (1).

items.stem: For the dimerisation of nitrogen dioxide, ΔH⦵ = −57 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS⦵ = −176 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Explain how temperature affects the spontaneity of the reaction.
items.answer: Spontaneous only below 324 K: at high T the positive −TΔS term outweighs the negative ΔH.
items.markingKey: Uses ΔG = ΔH − TΔS (1); spontaneous only below 324 K: at high T the positive −TΔS term outweighs the negative ΔH (2).

items.stem: For the thermite reaction, 2Al(s) + Fe₂O₃(s) → Al₂O₃(s) + 2Fe(s), ΔH⦵ = −852 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS⦵ = −38 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. What is ΔG at 298 K?
items.answer: −841 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: B. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = −852 − 298 × (−38/1000) = −841 kJ mol⁻¹. Forgetting to convert J to kJ is the common error.

items.stem: Using the standard entropy values (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) C₂H₅OH(l) 161, O₂(g) 205, CO₂(g) 214, H₂O(l) 70, determine the standard entropy change for C₂H₅OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l).
items.answer: −138 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: ΣS(products) = 638, ΣS(reactants) = 776 (M1, coefficients used); ΔS = −138 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (A1).

items.stem: For C₂H₄(g) + H₂(g) → C₂H₆(g), ΔH⦵ = −136 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS⦵ = −121 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Determine the temperature below which the reaction is spontaneous.
items.markingKey: Set ΔG = 0: T = ΔH/ΔS (M1) = −136/−0.121 (unit conversion) = 1120 K (A1); spontaneous below this temperature (A1).

items.stem: For the vaporisation of water, H₂O(l) → H₂O(g), ΔH⦵ = +44 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS⦵ = +119 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. What is ΔG at 500 K?
items.answer: −15.5 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: A. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = 44 − 500 × (119/1000) = −15.5 kJ mol⁻¹. Forgetting to convert J to kJ is the common error.

items.stem: Predict the sign of ΔS for 2NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g).
options: positive: the number of moles of gas decreases
negative: the number of moles of gas decreases
negative: the number of moles of gas increases
items.answer: negative: the number of moles of gas decreases
items.markingKey: B. Gas moles change by −1.

items.stem: At 700 K, ΔG⦵ for C₂H₄(g) + H₂(g) → C₂H₆(g) is −51.3 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the equilibrium constant K at this temperature and comment on the position of equilibrium. (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
items.answer: K = 6760; products favoured

items.stem: For the Contact process, 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g), ΔH⦵ = −198 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS⦵ = −187 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. What is ΔG at 1200 K?
items.answer: +26.4 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: D. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = −198 − 1200 × (−187/1000) = +26.4 kJ mol⁻¹. Forgetting to convert J to kJ is the common error.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Counting moles of gas is a reliable way to predict the sign of ΔS for a reaction."
items.answer: A good first approximation, but calculations with S⦵ values are needed when gas moles are equal or effects compete.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: gas entropy dominates, so the rule works for most reactions; quick qualitative prediction. Arguments against: fails when the number of gas moles is unchanged; dissolving, mixing and changes in molecular complexity also matter; quantitative ΔS requires standard entropies. Supported judgement: A good first approximation, but calculations with S⦵ values are needed when gas moles are equal or effects compete.

items.stem:
Consider the combustion of ethanol: C₂H₅OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l).

species | ΔHf⦵ / kJ mol⁻¹ | S⦵ / J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
C₂H₅OH(l) | −278 | 161
O₂(g) | 0 | 205
CO₂(g) | −394 | 214
H₂O(l) | −286 | 70

(a) Calculate ΔH⦵. (b) Calculate ΔS⦵. (c) Calculate ΔG at 1000 K and deduce whether the reaction is spontaneous. (d) Calculate the temperature at which the reaction becomes (or stops being) spontaneous.
items.answer: (a) −1370 kJ mol⁻¹; (b) −138 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; (c) −1230 kJ mol⁻¹, spontaneous; (d) 9910 K
items.markingKey: (a) ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants) = −1370 (A1). (b) −138 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (A1). (c) ΔG = ΔH − TΔS with ΔS in kJ (M1) = −1230 kJ mol⁻¹ (A1). (d) T = ΔH/ΔS = −1368/−0.138 = 9910 K (A1).

items.stem: Consider (I) CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l) and (II) CuO(s) + H₂(g) → Cu(s) + H₂O(l). (a) Predict the sign of ΔS for each, giving reasons. (b) Calculate ΔS⦵ for each using the data booklet standard entropies. (c) Explain which reaction shows the greater increase in disorder, and whether your predictions in (a) were correct.
items.answer: (b) I −242 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, II −71.0 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "standard Gibbs energy of formation".
items.answer: The Gibbs energy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states under standard conditions

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "entropy (S)"?

The temperature T = ΔH/ΔS at which ΔG = 0, above or below which the spontaneity of a reaction changes sign
A negative ΔG⦵ corresponds to K > 1 (products favoured); a positive ΔG⦵ corresponds to K < 1 (reactants favoured)
The relationship between the standard Gibbs energy change and the equilibrium constant at temperature T
items.answer: A measure of the dispersal of energy and matter in a system: the number of possible arrangements of particles and their energy
items.markingKey: A. "entropy (S)" is a measure of the dispersal of energy and matter in a system: the number of possible arrangements of particles and their energy.

items.stem: At equilibrium, which statement about ΔG is correct?
items.answer: ΔG = 0
items.markingKey: A. No further net change.

items.stem: Explain why an endothermic reaction can be spontaneous.
items.answer: If ΔS is positive and the temperature is high enough, the TΔS term exceeds ΔH, so ΔG = ΔH − TΔS becomes negative.

items.stem: Which substance has the highest standard entropy?
items.answer: C₃H₈(g)

items.stem: Distinguish between ΔG⦵ and ΔG.
items.answer: ΔG⦵ refers to standard conditions (all species at standard state) and determines K; ΔG refers to the actual mixture and becomes zero at equilibrium.

items.answer: Entropy decreases on cooling because particles have fewer accessible energy states; the sign of ΔS is not determined by ΔH.

items.stem: "ΔG⦵ values are sufficient to decide whether an industrial process is viable." Discuss.
items.answer: ΔG⦵ is a necessary first screen, but kinetics, equilibrium position under real conditions and economics decide viability.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: identify feasible reactions and favourable temperatures; link to equilibrium constants. Arguments against: rates may be far too slow without catalysts; real conditions are non-standard; costs, safety, yield and environmental factors are also decisive. Supported judgement: ΔG⦵ is a necessary first screen, but kinetics, equilibrium position under real conditions and economics decide viability. items.stem: Arrange in order of increasing standard entropy, giving reasons: H₂O(s), H₂O(l), H₂O(g), C(diamond), CH₄(g), C₃H₈(g).
